name: cuttlefish
desc: Build compacted de Bruijn graphs from references or reads
why: Builds compacted de Bruijn graphs from sequencing reads, real genomics software that is a close call for a home break.

brief.what_it_is: Cuttlefish 3 is a command-line tool that builds compacted de Bruijn graphs, where each vertex is a maximal unitig, from reference FASTA sequences or sequencing reads (FASTQ, gzipped input accepted). It can build an uncolored graph or a colored graph over a collection of genomes, and the colored output records which input sources cover which stretch of each unitig, written alongside the unitig FASTA. The binary also has commands for comparing graphs, querying colors, cleaning up, and probing.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as fast, parallel graph construction that stays feasible at collection scale, claiming it has built the colored graph of 150,000 bacterial genomes on a single machine. The homepage says the tool is designed for collections too large to keep in RAM.
brief.how_it_works: Partition buckets, blocked edge matrices, and collation buckets live on disk, so peak RAM tracks the worker set rather than the graph size. Partitioning, local contraction, discontinuity contraction, and final collation all run multi-threaded under a worker budget set by the user (the -t flag). The working directory passed with -w holds the intermediate external-memory files.

commands_seen.context: Homebrew install, one of three listed install routes alongside conda and cargo.

Builds an uncolored compacted graph from a reference FASTA, with k=31, 16 threads, work directory work/, and output prefix graph.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew, Bioconda, and prebuilt GitHub release binaries cover Linux and macOS on x86-64 and arm64. Building from source needs a Rust toolchain 1.91 or newer, either via cargo install cuttlefish-rs-cli or a git clone followed by cargo build --release. No accounts, licences to acquire, or runtimes beyond that were mentioned. The user supplies a work directory (-w) and thread count (-t) on each run; the README does not describe any configuration file.
brief.standout: It is a genomics graph builder rather than a typical developer tool, but it stands out for its external-memory design, which keeps RAM use tied to worker count instead of graph size, and for colored graphs over very large genome collections. The same project also keeps the older C++ Cuttlefish 1 and 2 on separate branches and docs, with separate papers.
brief.status: Maintained as far as the README shows. It describes version 3.1.0 as feature-complete and validated for odd k from 3 to 63, points to a CHANGELOG, and cites a RECOMB 2026 paper with a bioRxiv preprint. I did not see a release date or last-commit date, so recency beyond the version number is unknown.
brief.caveats: Aimed at bioinformaticians working with sequencing data; the homepage and README assume familiarity with de Bruijn graphs and unitigs. Prebuilt binaries are listed only for Linux and macOS, and Windows is not mentioned. Building from source needs Rust 1.91 or newer. The native-CPU build flag makes binaries non-portable. The README asks users to cite the paper. The license is BSD 3-Clause. Cuttlefish 1 and 2 (C++) are documented separately and are not covered by this entry's commands.
quotes: Fast, parallel, low-memory construction of compacted de Bruijn graphs — from reference sequences or sequencing reads, at collection scale.
it has built the colored graph of 150,000 bacterial genomes on a single machine.
Feature-complete and validated on reference and read inputs, uncolored and colored, for odd k from 3 to 63.
